abstract: The seed coat protects the embryo from environmental stresses while controlling important agricultural traits, such as seed dormancy, germination, and longevity. The Arabidopsis seed coat epidermal layer secretes a pectin-rich cell wall, the mucilage, which regulates seed hydration and germination. In the subepidermal layer, the lipid polyester suberin is deposited in the cell wall, where it forms a protective barrier against solutes and gases. Currently, the mechanisms coordinating the development of these important cell layers of the outer integument are poorly understood. Here, we show that NAC38 and NAC58 are preferentially expressed in the outer integument and directly promote the expression of FUSCA3 (FUS3), a master regulator of seed maturation that promotes fatty acid biosynthesis and desiccation tolerance. In a feedback loop, FUS3 positively regulates NAC38 and NAC58. Loss-of-function mutations in NAC38, NAC58, and FUS3 transcription factors affect the development of the outer integument, by reducing radial wall thickening and mucilage extrusion, while altering suberin monomer levels. Loss of FUS3 also decreases total suberin content, suggesting a prominent role for FUS3 in this process. During prolonged dry storage, loss of NAC38 decreases seedling growth and loss of NAC38 and NAC58 increase seed sensitivity to salinity stress. Genome-wide binding sites and transcriptomic analysis support a role for these transcription factors in cell wall-related processes, by directly regulating mucilage- and suberin-related genes, through shared and distinct gene sets. This study uncovered novel regulators of mucilage secretory cell differentiation and suberin monomers accumulation, which affect seed longevity and salt sensitivity of aged seeds
